summary: This article explains how Arabic poetry's rhyme, rhythm, and memory kept history and stories alive long before writing was widespread, and why it is still loved today.
introduce: Show the title “Arabic Poetry: Words with Rhythm” and give pairs one minute to list everything they already know about this topic. Share a few ideas on the board, then tell students to check which ideas the article confirms.

keyTerms.def: a regular pattern of beats in a line of poetry
a single line, or group of lines, in a poem
a long traditional Arabic poem built on one meter and one rhyme

challengeTerms.def: to keep something safe from being lost or damaged
traditions and knowledge passed down from earlier generations

discussion: Do you agree or disagree that stories are easier to remember when they are told with rhyme and rhythm? Use evidence from the article to explain.
Explain how a qasida was composed and recited, and why oral tradition mattered before writing was widespread.
struggling: Pre-teach meter, verse, and qasida with pictures or gestures, then let weak readers use a K-W-L chart and read the article with a partner.
gifted: Ask strong readers to read a challenging version and write a short paragraph that uses oral, preserve, and heritage to connect the article to something they learned in another subject.
